speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-174, to amend the Interest Act.

subtopic: PROPOSED LIMITATION OF RATE CHARGED ON REAL ESTATE MORTGAGES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROPOSED LIMITATION OF RATE CHARGED ON REAL ESTATE MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to limit the rate of interest that may be charged on mortgages of real estate in Canada. At the present time the great mass of the population are finding it increasingly difficult to acquire homes of their own, to a large extent because of the very high rates of interest that prevail across the country on mortgages of real estate, something that should not be necessary so far as secured creditors are concerned.
This bill is merely an attempt by a member of this house to amend the Interest Act to deal with the situation. Mortgages of real estate in which the principal moneys are made payable to the government of Canada or any crown corporation have had to be exempted from the provisions of the bill in order that a private member of parliament may not be barred by law from introducing the legislation.
I am sure the house will welcome an opportunity, brief though it may be, to have a discussion on the bill as a whole. This is an attempt to discipline a wayward economy-

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-175, to amend the Canadian Bill of Rights with respect to official languages.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING USE OF EITHER OFFICIAL LANGUAGE
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING USE OF EITHER OFFICIAL LANGUAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Bill of Rights is silent on the right of Canadian citizens to use both official languages. It appears highly desirable that Canadian citizens feel at home from coast to coast, and the purpose of this bill is to ensure that they be in a position to use either the English or the French language throughout the land. It is not the purpose of this bill to compel anyone to speak two languages, but to declare the practical equality of both languages. It is but one step in the direction of Canadian unity.

In answer to this question I would remind my hon. friend that in 1964 parliament enacted the 12 mile fishing zone limit with the provision that a straight base line system should be adopted by Canada. This is now the law of the land. This system is being implemented by Canada in a way which takes into account the treaty and traditional fishing rights of other countries, including the United States.
The action taken by Canada follows precedents set by many countries including Norway, Iceland, Britain, Denmark, Ireland and many others. The United States has had consultations with Canada. They knew of the steps we were proposing to take. I understand fully the nature of the statement made by the United States yesterday, but this is a matter in which I am afraid friendly countries may have to disagree.

Mr. Chairman, I thought at the outset we would have a statement of some kind from the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Perhaps he has decided to wait until he has heard the remarks of hon. members before making such a statement, but a statement of this kind would be of benefit to hon. members during the consideration of his estimates, and if he should like the opportunity to make one now I will be glad to take my seat.
October 27, 1967

Apparently the minister does not wish to make a statement now. Members on this side are somewhat disappointed at the lack of factual information emanating from the minister's department. Several days ago I asked the Prime Minister whether it would be possible to have the Wood commission report made available before discussing these estimates. Evidently that was not possible, but the tabling of even an interim report would make the discussion of these estimates easier. We have been waiting for more than a year and a half for the results of this inquiry.
It is my opinion that a general overhaul should be made of pension legislation. This legislation has not been amended for quite a few years. It was originally brought forward in a hurry to expedite assistance to veterans who had completed their wartime service. In light of what has transpired in the last few years a general review of veterans pension legislation should be made.
Hon. members who were members of the veterans affairs committee made suggestions as to how the act should be amended. I am sure the minister has taken those suggestions into consideration, but as of this date nothing constructive has been done in this regard. There has been difficulty in respect of liaison between the minister and his staff, but I understand this situation has been remedied. Perhaps some action will be taken soon.
It was also my thought that following the analytical study of pension legislation in other countries, specifically France and Britain, a new assessment could be made of the available information on our own legislation.
I understand there was anticipation that a review of United States studies on veterans legislation would be made, but so far as I am aware this has not been done yet. Perhaps this information could be used in conjunction with the Wood commission report. Certainly some effort should be made to correlate the information which is available at the present time in respect of this important information.
I presume the representations and appeals made from time to time to the minister and the department by various organizations have been considered. We would like to hear what is in store for our veterans in the next year. The cost of living has made it imperative that increases in pensions be considered and now would be a good time to let our veterans know what they can expect in the future.

Supply-Veterans Affairs [DOT] (12 noon)
I do not intend to cover the whole spectrum of veterans affairs because my colleagues will wish to make contributions. However, when the minister makes a statement I believe he should be somewhat explicit in so far as the control of veterans hospitals is concerned. There has been considerable controversy about the situation at Sunnybrook hospital. I should like to put on record parts of an article written for the Toronto Telegram of September 23 last by Peter Ward, who evidently studied the situation at that hospital. If the situation that has developed there is going to be prevalent at other hospitals, something should be done to prevent this happening. In his article Mr. Ward said:
You can list grievances by the hundred, many of them chronic complaints from chronic complainers, but an alarming number that are real, legitimate beefs.
Under D.V.A. administration veterans were issued prescribed drugs at the hospital dispensary and if treatment was lengthy for outpatients, drugs would be mailed as needed to the patient.
Now the veteran must either convince his local pharmacy to hand over prescribed drugs and bill D.V.A., or pay for them himself and collect later.
Usually it's much later. Due to staff shortages, it's sometimes more than three months before a druggist, or a veteran who has paid, gets his money.
Under D.V.A., hospital patients had the option of eating meals either in their rooms or in the dining room, if they were able, with buddies.
Now they eat in their rooms. They can eat in the dining room only if they pay for their meals.
This writer goes on to list other complaints, and the article continues:
The daily Sunnybrook patient rate when U. of T. took over was $23.25. It went to $36 daily immediately and is now $40. Treatment of pensionable veterans, or those earning less than $1,296 annually, was free then, and still is.
Any veteran is guaranteed a bed at Sunnybrook, pensionable or not. If he isn't pensionable, a patient must pay his bill either personally or through insurance. That's still the same, only the rate has changed.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit me to interrupt him for a moment at this time?
Certainly.

With reference to this story, Mr. Chairman, I do not think it should be allowed to go on the record without some comment. All the complaints received, and there have not been that many, have been investigated and most of this story has been
Oclober 27, 1967

Supply-Veterans Affairs found to be quite unfounded. Nothing occurring at Sunnybrook hospital now did not occur before the changeover. I want that fact to be underlined. I am sure the hon. member will appreciate that the story to which he has referred does need correction.

This article was written just about a month ago. If the Department of Veterans Affairs had been as speedy in investigating other matters as it was in this case there would have been no complaints at all, but obviously there was some ground for complaint. If the situation has been remedied, we appreciate the action that has been taken. There have been rumours that the other hospitals now operated by D.V.A. will fall into the hands of provincial or municipal bodies, and I think this committee is entitled to know whether any plans of that nature are in prospect.
Over the last year and a half many representations have been made to the minister and his department to give us some outline of what can be expected in the nature of veterans legislation. I hope that today the minister will afford himself of the opportunity to deal with this question and will give us some idea of what we may expect in the future.

Mr. Chairman, would the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who has done so much to help the veterans and their families, tell us when the legislation mentioned in vote 17a will become effective, or on what date will the benefits be available to the people themselves?

Mr. Chairman, I have brief remarks to make on a number of subjects connected with these estimates. First of all I should like to extend to the minister publicly my personal appreciation for his invitation to have me participate in the commemorative exercises this summer on the twenty fifth anniversary of the Dieppe raid. I should also like to commend the officers of his department for

Would the hon. gentleman permit me to interrupt him at this moment? The point I would like to make clear is that the ceremonies were organized primarily by the municipal authorities at Dieppe and we were only participants. The Canadian government as such did not interfere in one way or another with the participation of German forces at the ceremony, nor do I believe that the French or the British governments interfered. This was left entirely to the local people, who undoubtedly were influenced by the public comments made in Canada.

I wonder whether the minister would be prepared to tell the house why
October 27, 1967	COMMONS DEBATES	3569
the government did not even acknowledge the letter requesting German participation. I know there were letters asking for this. I can tell the minister privately about some conversations I had in this respect which are of a more confidential nature. We in Canada missed a great opportunity, and that is all I will say about it.
There is another matter about which I would like to say a few words. It also concerns prisoners of war. Some time ago I placed a question on the order paper asking whether the treatment section of the Department of Veterans Affairs intended to call in prisoners of war through the various treatment centres in the country to give them a check-over either there or through the facilities of the Canadian pension commission. I consider this to be treatment of a preventive nature. There is no use waiting for a veteran to come in and say: I am ill and this is attributable to a disability incurred during the war. The minister is in the same position as I am. We are both former prisoners of war. He will recall the agitation on both sides of the house with regard to the Hong Kong prisoners of war. I think that finally the right steps were taken on their behalf and none too soon. However, I suggest to him that the same applies to other prisoners of war whose medical histories after incarceration have followed the same pattern.
Relatively speaking the minister and I did not suffer too much, but I know of many men who had to subsist for long periods of time on raw sugar beets which they pulled out of frozen fields. How has this affected them? We are not able to say whether any of these men who have died may have done so five or ten years earlier than they should have. And yet what do we know about those who are still suffering from the effects of the war? I think that here again we are missing an opportunity. I am sure that the treatment services have learned a great deal from the examinations of the Hong Kong prisoners of war conducted in the past few years. The same could be done with all the other prisoners of war. This is what I would call a form of preventive medicine. Their experiences cannot be duplicated. After all, there are not that many of these men who may serve as guinea-pigs, and experiments cannot be conducted easily with regard to this type of condition. I strongly urge the minister to reconsider the position taken by his department in the reply to my question. I really feel that we are passing up a truly worthwhile opportunity.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
The next point I want to make is that I also had the opportunity to visit Vimy this year and, having acquainted myself with some of the problems which exist with regard to the maintenance of the memorial and the park there, I strongly urge the minister, even though he may run into some difficulties with the Minister of Finance, to consider the building of a diversionary road around the park. At present the road going through the park makes the maintenance of the memorial and the surrounding grounds very difficult for the limited staff that we have there on holidays and week ends. Since in France the week end is from Saturday noon to Tuesday morning on long week ends the Vimy park is much like Coney Island. People come from the surrounding villages and towns and gather on the lawns for picnics. They lay out the laundry on the grass and do all sorts of things. If we relocated the road and made an arrangement with the French government so that route nationale No. 37 going through the park could be moved, I think it would make it much simpler for everyone concerned. I think it would also make for less strained relations between the Canadian authorities at Vimy and the mayors and councillors of the neighboring towns.
The next point on which I would like to say a few words is in connection with the War Veterans Allowance Act and the inability of the government at the present time to consider the payment of war veterans allowances to many Canadian veterans living in the United Kingdom who are in great need of assistance and cannot afford to come back to put in the required one year of residence in Canada. There has been an extensive exchange of correspondence between Lieutenant Colonel Jones, the president of the Canadian Army Veterans in the United Kingdom Association, and officials of the minister's department. Frankly, all they are doing is setting up administrative obstacles. I have spoken to some of the officials who were in the department at the time when I headed it and they say this is not so. I admit that there is a division of opinion. It is said that there may be possibilities of overpayments which would create grave difficulties in trying to collect such overpayments. However, surely it is unreasonable to say that the department should not institute such a program because of possible difficulties in having to recover overpayments. I do not think the minister could or would seriously
3570	COMMONS
Supply-Veterans Affairs justify such an argument. The basis of that argument is wrong.
Canadian veterans who either served in world war I or world war II and who have in some cases come on more difficult times are not being paid war veterans allowances because they married in the United Kingdom and have not returned to Canada or have remained there for reasons of health. Yet allied veterans who come to Canada and live here for ten years qualify for the war veterans allowance and receive it. They may live here for another year and then decide to take off for Florida, the United Kingdom or France. If they do we in Canada continue to pay them. I do not think there is true justice in such a situation. It is the requirement of one year's residence that is the bogey. I would ask the minister to eliminate this continuing farce because it is truly a farcical situation but in so many instances it has tragic consequences.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
This summer when I went to London I took a number of files in connection with widows or veterans who are experiencing difficult times as I wanted to have them examined to see what could be done. The stumbling block was the statutory year's residence in Canada for the men involved. If there is one acceptable principle for the payment of the war veterans allowance it is war service. Evidently we are prepared to pay this allowance to servicemen of our allies who reside in Canada for ten years and then go back to the United Kingdom or elsewhere. We pay it to them there because they served and then came to Canada and spent ten years here. However, if a Canadian veteran stayed in the United Kingdom, married and worked there, he receives nothing. His entitlement to war veterans allowance should not arise from his residence in Canada but as a result of his war service. I believe that should be the principle.
With these remarks, Mr. Chairman, I draw to a close my intervention in this debate. There are some other points I should like to raise on another occasion, but I know that a number of my colleagues want to say a few words. I hope these few points I have mentioned will merit favourable consideration by the minister and his officials.

Before proceeding with my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I want to support the hon. member for Edmonton West in his plea for veterans residing in Great Britain or other allied countries. They should not be

DEBATES	October 27, 1967
required to return to Canada to live for a year in order to qualify for war veterans allowance. As the minister knows we heard representations from organizations in Great Britain as well as in France, Belgium and Holland. They all had the same attitude toward this question. Like the hon. member, I cannot see any reason for asking them to return to Canada when the allowance is awarded on the basis of war service. I do hope the government will give consideration to the representations in this respect.
At the present time the major concern of veterans in Canada is an increase in the disability pension and the war veterans allowance. It is obvious that this does concern veterans and their dependants and veterans organizations. In order to indicate the extent of their concern I show the minister the over 100 letters I have received to date on this issue. There is a regular campaign going on in Kootenay West. We have ten branches of the Royal Canadian Legion. I will give the minister the letters later, but they show the interest in this question and the need for increases.
Our whole system of judging the rate of pension is wrong. In the first instance it was based on the wage of a casual labourer. The increases in pensions have not been equal to the increases received by casual labourers thus far. This is the first reason for discontent. The second reason is the rapid increase in the cost of living during the last two or three years. I believe these arguments are soundly based.
Canada has a generally good record with regard to veterans legislation. However, we are reaching a stage now where we have to approach our problems in this field on an international basis rather than on a strictly national basis. Before I sit down I want to bring to the attention of the members of the committee what has been done in this respect. I happen to be a member of the World Veterans Federation which has done a lot of constructive work in respect of improving veterans legislation generally in all countries of the world. I know that members of the Legion and veterans who will receive a copy of Hansard containing this day's proceedings will want to know something about what has been done. I should like, therefore, to place a few facts on the record.
This organization, one might say, is the counterpart of the International Labour Organization, The World Federation of Farm Women, the World Health Organization and
October 27, 19S7

organizations of that type which have resulted from the realization that if we are going to solve our problems satisfactorily we have to solve them almost on the basis of an international set of rules. This is what has been done to date. The organization has held its third conference on legislation with regard to veterans affairs. Under the heading "International Documentation on Benefits for War Victims", the conference recommended the assembling by all means at its disposal, with the assistance of governments and member associations, of the fullest possible data bearing on the establishment of valid comparisons of the purchasing power of national currencies, gross national revenues, national budgets, average wages and the number of war victims in receipt of benefits in relation both to the amount of benefits granted and to modifications of legislation in this field. I believe that suggestion was made as a result of considerable thought.
The second heading was "Co-operation in Promoting Veterans Protection". The conference called upon veterans organizations and competent governmental institutions pursuing humanitarian aims for the protection of veterans and their dependants to develop comprehensive mutual co-operation for the purpose of completing and improving systems of protection of veterans, resistants and war victims.
The next subject was "Indemnification for Damages and Illnesses Resulting Indirectly from Disabilities Already Giving Entitlement to Indemnification". The conference recommended that governments ensure the indemnification of any aggravation occuring in the somatic state of a person disabled in war or while performing military service, not only when it is established medically that his recognized lesions or sicknesses were caused exclusively by a disability previously recognized as being war or service connected but also where a consensus of medical opinion makes it possible to consider that the predominant cause of the new disability is the accepted war disablement. They recommended also the introduction into the legislation of countries concerned of provisions which make possible a benevolent, clear and uniform application of the relevant regulations.
The conference also discussed the discrimination existing against the less severely disabled in the matter of pensions and advocated scales of pensions proportional to disability ratings. There was a recommendation that the governments concerned resist any such tendency, accord to the less severely disabled

Supply-Veterans Affairs their true worth and respect their rights and, with this end in view, ensure that scales of pensions are directly proportional to the basic pension related to the medical assessment of the disablement.
The conference then dealt with the influence of age on war pension rates. They called upon governments to introduce, where necessary, legislation whereby the disabled are entitled to the undiminished rate of their disability pension as from the age of 60, or earlier in cases where they have been in receipt of such pensions for a period of ten years.
The next subject dealt with was the adjustment of war victims pensions. The conference went on to recommend that governments establish pensions and other benefits in line with rising national standards.
The next heading is "The Exemption of War Pensions from Tax". The conference recommended that the governments concerned should decide that the compensation provided war victims by legislation should be exempted from tax. Our legislation has always done this so we are ahead of others in that respect.
Then there was a recommendation in connection with cars driven by the disabled. In fact, there is quite a lengthy list of recommendations in this connection, all of which should be given consideration by governments.
The conference then dealt with measures on behalf of the disabled regarding pension revision procedures. The recommendation was that governments go into all aspects of pension revision procedures. I understand that is exactly what the government is supposed to be doing at the present time, devising a formula for the rates of pension to be paid.
The next heading is "Benefits for Dependants of the Severely War Disabled Irrespective of the Cause of Death". The conference called upon governments to guarantee benefits for the dependants of the severely war disabled, irrespective of the cause of the latter's death.
The conference also dealt with benefits for the parents of war victims and recommended that governments compensate them adequately for their loss.

In the matter of compensation for exclusion from social security benefits it was recommended that governments concerned introduce legislation to this end.

They then discussed the reckoning of periods of wartime service for social insurance purposes and made a recommendation in that regard. Recommends that the draft charter of veterans basic rights be referred back to the executive board of the W.V.F. for consideration by an expert committee who, taking into full consideration the draft memoranda already agreed by the members of the charter subcommittee should also take account of the recommendations and conclusions of the third international legislation conference in the preparation of the ultimate draft, and that in its preamble the final draft should specifically define those groups of persons for whom the special rights and privileges are required, noting that the rights of war veterans proclaimed by the charter be equally applied to the members of the resistance as to the category of war veterans.
I have made reference to these recommendations, Mr. Chairman, because this conference was a very interesting one. Assembled there were members of veterans organizations from practically every country in the world and they were meeting together to discuss common problems affecting veterans legislation in their own countries. As I said before, I think that if we are to get some sort of world rule of law in this respect and to do justice to all persons affected by war-veterans, their dependants, victims of war and so on-more and more we must approach the subject from, shall I say, an international point of view.
When the members of the standing committee on veterans affairs were overseas they met with representatives of various veterans groups in France, Belgium, Holland and Great Britain. We also had the opportunity of discussing veterans legislation and its relationship to social legislation with some representatives of the ministry of pensions in Great Britain, and we had a very informative session. I mention this because I am quite sure there are many people in Canada who are unaware of the constructive and co-operative work being done in this regard in order to direct attention to the problems of veterans, their dependants, victims of aggression and so on throughout the world so that they receive justice on a wider and wider scale as the years go by.

Before the estimates are passed I shall be looking forward to a very definitive statement from the minister which will cheer the hearts of all Canadian veterans and their

dependants, as well as all veterans organizations, prior to our recognition of Remembrance day.

The most important topic before us is the care of our pensioners of the first world war, second world war and the Korea war. We do not pay enough attention to our pensioners. Quite properly, we have a standing committee on veterans affairs and that committee works effectively. The minister who heads the department must give leadership in these matters and my criticism of the minister is that in the last three years when he has presented his estimates to the House of Commons he has spoken for about two or three minutes simply to say that as his estimates had been before a committee there was no need to discuss them extensively in the house. Hear, hear.

tendency is to consider it unimportant. The grave danger which faces the veterans of Canada is that with the passage of time people generally will tend to forget them. There is a new generation coming up. Fortunately it has been free from having to make sacrifices in warfare, but that new generation should be interested in the history of our country, should know something of the fight for freedom that was carried on by its predecessors and should be steeled in its own will to face similar hazards if called upon to do so.

Let us not carelessly brush aside or treat as something insignificant the care of our disabled veterans. The minister should have put the figures on the record to show the number of people still suffering. Why did he not say that of the approximately 33,000 disabled pensioners of the first world war almost 6,000 are men who are in the category of 75 per cent to 100 per cent disability? Mr. Chairman, just before the luncheon adjournment I was dealing with some of the problems that affect the veterans of this country and attempting to place some emphasis on the responsibilities which should weigh on the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the government generally. In the few minutes I have left at my disposal this afternoon I should like to stress the importance of the history of this country and this history of the world in which our countrymen have been involved.
We deplore war in any form, but the history of the world is largely a history of warfare and our country has been most active in this history. Whether we like it or not, the type of world in which we have lived during the twentieth century has subjected Canadians to the pressures of international affairs. Canadians have responded in time of danger and trouble and have stood shoulder to shoulder with freedom-loving men from every country.
During this our centennial year nothing has been more appropriate to my mind than the writing and publishing of a book by Hon. Leslie Frost. He is a very distinguished Canadian, a former premier of the province of Ontario and a serving soldier during the first world war. He has accomplished something unique in military history as a result of
October 27, 1967

Supply-Veterans Affairs telling about the part in that war played by men from Orillia. The story of the men from this community can be duplicated in respect of small hamlets, villages, towns, communities and cities from coast to coast in Canada. Men from these areas played a similar part during that war. I commend this book to everyone in Canada. Anyone who reads it will understand what took place in communities across this country like Orillia at the time of that confrontation. The foreword to this book was written by the president of Trent University, Thomas H. B. Symons. I should like to read the second paragraph:
The book tells the story of a group of men-the 393 members of the 35th Regiment of Simcoe Foresters who came forward for military service from the Orillia community half a century ago-and of the impact of the first world war upon them and their families and their community, and it does so with great perception and understanding. But it is more than a narrative of events. It is a statement of the author's faith in his country and some of his deeply felt convictions about this country.
At page 139 Mr. Frost has written the following:
One of the great tragedies of Canadian history has been our failure to translate into Canadian pride and loyalty the accomplishments of her men in the tragic period of the war. The achievements of the Canadian Corps from the day of the first landing in France in 1915 until the day of victory, should be a reason for pride on the part of all Canadians. It is a fantastic story. The Canadian Army Corps commenced with the enlistment in August, 1914 of men garbed in red coats and blue trousers. On the 14th of that month Orillia's contribution to the new Canadian expeditionary force marched down Mississaga street. This story was repeated in communities all across Canada. It was the beginning of the organization of an army corps which was second to none on the western front, or any other front. It became an unsurpassed fighting machine. Its accomplishments were outstanding. The bravery, the brain, the brawn and the ability to adapt to unforeseen conditions, should be an inspiration to all Canadians. Unfortunately, in the twenties and thirties, when democracy seemed to lose its purpose and direction, the Canadian people and their governments seemed to play down these monumental achievements of their countrymen. Perhaps, 50 years later in 1967 at the time of the one hundredth birthday of our country, some of the robust sentiments of the past can be regained.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Children of other days sang with pride and enthusiasm about Queenston Heights and Lundy's Lane, and about their forebears who "firmly stood and nobly died," in defence of their country. There is virtue in these days in remembering the men of Canada who firmly stood and nobly died in an even greater cause, the laying of the foundations of world government, which must exist if mankind is to survive.
Throughout the book one finds the story of these 393 men, their sacrifice, their devotion to duty, the honours they gained, the death


and the wounding of many of them, and their return to the homeland. That story of sacrifice and devotion to duty had to be repeated by their sons in the second great world war. This is now part and parcel of Canada's history and we should do honour to these men who made our country.
I grow weary of those people who are now searching for a Canadian identity. As I have said before in this house, Canada's identity as a nation was discovered and proved on the battlefields of Europe from 1914 to 1918. It was then that we emerged as a nation in the eyes of the world. Our representatives sat in at the peace keeping activities leading to the treaty of Versailles and in the formulation of the plans for the League of Nations. So when some people are searching now, 50 years later, for a Canadian identity I wonder at the lack of knowledge of Canadian history among those who write in that vein.
Part of our recognition of Canada's identity is to be found on those occasions when we pay tribute to those who lost their lives in the various wars. We have been doing this now for 50 years in Canada on various occasions. During the last several years we have been participating in commemorative memorial services in Europe, and I think these should be continued. It was only proper that we should recognize, as we did, the twenty fifth anniversary of the battle of Dieppe. I think it is only proper that we should recognize other episodes in the course of the second world war and similarly we should recognize episodes in the first world war.
Of course it will soon be time for a stand-down with regard to the first world war. After all, when the fiftieth anniversary is involved there are not many left who can participate in such a ceremony. I recall that a few years ago we held a ceremony here in Ottawa to commemorate the sixtieth anniversary of the conclusion of the South African war. Some very distinguished veterans of that war paraded here and participated under government auspices in a ceremony to pay honour to their contribution in that strife. They were then all in the eighties.
So by the time you hit the fiftieth anniversary you are coming pretty well to the end of the road. But it is only right that we should participate in ceremonies of that nature in order to recognize the sacrifices of the first world war and in order to recognize the history of our country. Therefore it was with great pleasure that I heard of the plans for
October 27, 1967	COMMONS
the ceremony at Vimy Ridge in the spring of this year. I was glad that Canada participated in the recognition of the fiftieth anniversary of that battle. I was pleased to be able to attend the ceremony at Passchendaele just a few weeks ago when once again Canada recognized one of the important battles of the first world war. Sixteen thousand young Canadian men either lost their lives or were wounded in that conflict, but they achieved their objective.
From 50 years ago yesterday up to November 10 represents the period when the Canadian Corps was engaged in the third battle of Ypres which culminated in the battle of Passchendaele. We were engaged in that battle 50 years ago, and 50 years ago today a former distinguished member of this house, now the Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia, Hon. George Pearkes, was awarded the Victoria Cross for his valour in that conflict.
Hear, hear.

It was only fitting that we should be there to pay our tribute, together with other members of the commonwealth, to those who fought in that struggle. The British, Australians, New Zealanders, South Africans, representatives from India and other portions of what was then known as the British Empire and Commonwealth, took part in the third battle of Ypres at the excessive cost of 150,000 casualties over a period of about three and a half months.
Just a few days ago there was at Tynecot cemetery in Belgium a ceremony at which we were present. Lord Alexander, former Governor General of Canada, was in charge of the ceremony and gave the address. My only complaint is that although there was a guard of honour provided by the United Kingdom, Belgium and France and a small guard of honour provided by Australia, there was no Canadian guard of honour. My complaint, which I hesitate to raise but I think I must do so, is that if we are to participate in ceremonies of this nature we should do it in the proper fashion.
Canada on that occasion should have had an appropriate guard of honour along with those countries which were our comrades in arms in the first great world war. The flimsy excuse that because the Canadian Brigade in Germany was engaged in NATO exercises and men could not be spared does not make much sense to those of us who have been in the services. It would be very unusual not to be able to spare one officer and 25 men for a
DEBATES	3577
Supply-Veterans Affairs guard of honour even if we could not have a guard of honour of 200. But the fact that Canada was not represented there is not, I think, good for Canada's prestige in international affairs.
If we participate in other functions of this nature, let us be very careful to see that we are properly represented, because when Canada is abroad other countries watch and see what we do. At the commemoration of the battle of Passchendaele, which was the Canadian portion of the third battle of Ypres, we did not have the appropriate public recognition by having a guard of honour there. I hope that next year, 1968-this might be the final ceremony for the first world war representing the 50th anniversary of the conclusion of that contest-we will be properly represented at some ceremony in Europe.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I hope there will be a Canadian organized ceremony at the city of Mons which the Canadians entered and seized on November 11, 1918. Others may have other ideas but I throw this out as one which occurs to me as being appropriate. To my mind Mons is the place where we should have the ceremony representing the fiftieth anniversary of the conclusion of the first world war. I hope that in 1969 we will appropriately join our comrades from Great Britain, the United States, France and all other countries that were involved in commemorating the beginning of the end of the second world war when the landings took place in Normandy in 1944. At the same time I hope the activities of Canadians in Sicily and Italy and in other parts of the world will not be overlooked.
These ceremonies are not numerous but they are very important. They tend to focus attention upon the history of our country. They acquaint the younger generation with the sacrifices that have been made in order to maintain freedom, and therefore we should not dismiss ceremonies of this nature just because we are all anxious for peace. No one is more anxious for peace in this world than men who have served in wartime, but at the same time we should recognize the sacrifices which a country makes in times of war.
This is all part of our history. This is how we have become a nation, and every child, every young man and young woman across this country should know the history of Canada. The two world wars and the war in Korea are part of it. There is a psychological effect involved. I hope the young people of
3578	COMMONS
Supply-Veterans Affairs today will not have to go through the experiences of the young people of 25 or 50 years ago but perhaps the reminder of these events will instil in them the right spirit if danger threatens so that they will respond in the same way as did their fathers, their grandfathers and their relatives. Thus the strength of the country will be maintained and not dissipated by all the emphasis which is put these days on the dangers of war and the fearful catastrophe which war can bring. We know all that, it is in our history, but at the same time we know that if freedom is to be maintained we have to be strong in spirit and determined to put forth the necessary effort no matter what the sacrifices may be.

Mr. Chairman,
there are a couple of brief matters which I would like to raise today in discussing the minister's estimates. Neither of them is new. We have raised them before but apparently we will have to keep raising them until something is done about them. The first one has to do with the long awaited Woods report.
I should like to read two paragraphs from a letter I received today on this very matter:
Apparently the "two language bit" is still their excuse for delay of this report; but that was their excuse, as you told me, over a year ago.
If the bureaucracies can use this as a further lot of red tape to delay action on justice, we would be better off without the two languages. I feel quite sure that any veterans in Quebec or elsewhere, who speak French, would gladly accept this report in English-just so its recommendations could be implemented.
The most significant thing about this letter is that it is signed by a Madame Boisvert. Ce n'est pas un nom anglais ga; c'est un nom canadien frangais. I know that what I am now saying has been said many times, but I think it bears repeating.
I think the department and the veterans affairs committee have been strictly non-partisan, but I noted today what I thought was a tenseness in the requests put before the minister. We have certainly not been partisan in the house today. Every party has called for action to improve the situation of our veterans. I have listened to every word that has been said in this chamber since the beginning of the debate, and every hon. member who has spoken has asked the minister to do something now. The last speaker put it very strongly. I am wondering whether it could be put more strongly. However, Mr. Chairman, I want to add my views to what has been said and say to the minister that he must use his power and energy to convince his cabinet colleagues that action must be taken, and quickly, in respect of the two matters that have been stressed, namely, the Woods commission report and the study of pension rates.
No one will do anything, let alone translate the report from English to French, if requests made by the minister are not backed up with punch and drive. The minister is in the happy position of being Minister of Veterans Affairs, but he is in the unhappy position of not providing the necessary punch and drive to produce the translation of the report and have completed the necessary research into the situation with regard to pension rates.
I rise in the debate to stress this one point, Mr. Chairman, because I have heard it said that the minister is just sitting, hoping he will not have to give answers to these questions because he will be moved to the Senate. Perhaps this is the reason why action has not been taken. But these important questions


should have been answered and the minister should not stall from day to day.
One can go back over Hansard of the last three years to find evidence of stalling by the minister, but I will give a recent example. On September 25 last the minister said, as reported at page 2463 of Hansard:
The Woods committee report will apparently be in my hands within a day or two, although not translated.
I emphasize the word "apparently." Why in the world does the minister not say: I want that report on my desk, and I am going to get it? I know that a commissioner cannot be ordered about, but the letter sent to the speaker who preceded me said that the minister had the report in his hands. On a subject so important as this why cannot the minister use that energy and drive that we all hope he will use some day to have the report produced? Why cannot he tell his cabinet colleagues that he is in a rough spot in this regard, has been stalling the veterans since 1963 when he was appointed Minister of Veterans Affairs, and something must be done to correct this situation?
I have drawn attention to that one passage in Hansard but I am quite sure that if the minister's secretary, his parliamentary secretary or anybody in his office cares to look back into the record they will find a great many answers which might give the minister the right to the title "the manana minister". It has always been tomorrow; and if not tomorrow, in just a few days.
I said that we have a non-partisan committee. The only reason I use strong language like that is that I believe the minister has it within his power to act on these matters for the benefit of our veterans. I believe he has to get cracking and do something. All the speeches made today have stressed the fact that action has been requested not only by members of parliament but by those who appeared before the committee in the last three of four years, and from veterans organizations from all over the country. They are demanding that action be taken.

Mr. Chairman, I also should like to say a few words about the treatment of war veterans allowance recipients. I do not intend to repeat the arguments that have been advanced with respect to the guaranteed income supplement because they have been well put by a number of speakers today. I would remind the minister, however, that when we were debating the legislation respecting the guaranteed income supplement some of us pointed out the unfairness that has now developed. What is most annoying about this is not merely that it happens but the way in which it happens. The war veterans allowance recipient who is an old age pensioner received two documents earlier this year, one of which was an application form for the guaranteed income supplement. It came to him from a department of the government of Canada and it had on it in large red print the information that war pensions or war veterans allowances did not preclude him from receiving the guaranteed income supplement. He was encouraged by the wording of that form, he was encouraged by the wording in the booklet that came with it, to apply for the guaranteed income supplement. The minister has pointed out, quite rightly, that his department advised the same war veterans allowance recipient that he should check with his local war veterans allowance officer. However, that advice was in a much less attractive document. It was typewritten, mimeographed or something like that and it was in fine print. Many veterans did not see that, and I am sure they saw just the red type invitation to apply for the guaranteed income supplement.

The people who are writing to me about it are using some pretty strong language about it.
As the War Veterans Allowance Act stands, a war veterans allowance recipient who is receiving the old age pension and who gets the extra $1.50 old age security increase will have $1.50 cut off his war veterans allowance. If he is one of those who has already applied for the guaranteed income supplement and is getting the pension and the supplement to the full amount of $105 per month, and if he has already gone through the indignity of suffering the loss of some of his war veterans allowance, he will get an increase of $2.10 in his old age pension; but $2.10 will come off his war veterans allowance unless the minister does something about it. We are talking about very small amounts, I know-of $1.50 or $2.10. The minister might well say to me, why take the time of the committee to talk about it. However, the fact is that another instance of this kind is going to be a bitter pill for many of these veterans to swallow.
I point out this difference between what will happen with respect to the $1.50 or the $2.10 in respect of the guaranteed income supplement. In the case of the guaranteed income supplement, the veteran who was receiving the old age pension had to apply for the supplement. He could be told, "You did not read all the words, you did not discover in advance what would happen". But he had to apply for it. In the case of the $1.50 or the $2.10, there is no application to be made; it is automatic. It will be there in his January cheque, and as I say, unless the minister does something about it, it will come off his allowance. I am sure, from the way in which the minister has been answering me with friendly facial expressions while I have been talking, that he is aware of how difficult this will be and how unfair it will be. Chairman, a number of departmental programs were discussed. Since it seems to be the wish of hon. members I might mention certain of those activities in order to give the committee an indication of the broad spectrum of programs in which the department is engaged.
In the research and development field my department has a number of programs, including the program for the advancement of industrial technology under which the development of commercial products is assisted, the defence export development program for the development of products of a military nature, the new Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act, and the industrial research institute program which has been established to foster greater cooperation between the business community and the universities in carrying out research and development.
Hon. members, I am sure, are most familiar with the automative program, the adjustment assistance program, the area development program, the industry modernization for defence exports program, the shipbuilding program, the design program and our program to improve the productivity of the building equipment, accessories and materials manufacturing industry.
I do not propose at this time to make a lengthy statement on these programs, except to say that the results to date are most gratifying. If hon. members wish to have a copy of the statement I made last June in committee, in which each of these activities is dealt with at some length, I would be most happy to provide it to them. However, I thought it might be more useful if I made a brief statement on the over-all operations of the department in order to provide as much time as possible for any questions hon. members may have.
As an economic department of government with particular responsibility for promoting the establishment and growth of manufacturing and processing industries in Canada on an efficient and competitive basis, the Department of Industry has as its principal mission the enhancement of the productivity performance of Canada's industrial economy.
In our form of economic system the role of government in the industrial development field has traditionally been limited to the application of broad economic policies of a commercial, fiscal or monetary nature. More recently Canada has recognized the need for industry and government to work more 27053-228
Supply-Industry
closely together in focussing on specific economic and technological problems, and in formulating mutually acceptable solutions which are beneficial to the economy as a whole.
With the establishment of the Department of Industry the government has created an instrument which can contribute directly to the attainment of this objective. With its mandate from parliament to acquire a detailed knowledge of manufacturing industries in Canada, and to develop and carry out programs to promote the establishment, growth, efficiency and improvement of these industries, my department has recruited and developed a group of professionals to formulate and implement imaginative programs to bring about constructive changes in Canadian industrial thinking and practice.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Our initial years of operation were characterized by recruitment of staff, policy and program formulation and the implementation and initial operation of a few important programs. The estimates for the fiscal year 196768 reflect the maturing of several programs and their growing utilization by the Canadian industrial community. In addition, the estimates reflect the consolidation within the Department of Industry of existing government industrial development programs. Of the total increase in our estimates for the fiscal year 1967-68 over fiscal year 1966-67 amounting to $95.8 million, almost $70 million is accounted for by transferred programs, while $27 million covers the requirement for increases in existing programs.
These amounts of money, while large, should not be regarded merely as expenditures. Rather, they should be looked upon as investments, of both time and money, in upgrading the productivity and competitive position of our industries. It is from this source, it should be remembered, that will come the improvements in wages and salaries, profits and tax revenues for all levels of government required to pay for all those things in the private and public sectors which Canadians have come to expect from our society.
In examining the estimates of the Department of Industry, it may be helpful for this committee to see them in the context of the department's mission and the basic approach it has developed for carrying it out. My approach and the approach of my departmental managers is to test each and every proposal which comes before us from outside

October 27, 1967
Supply-Industry
or from within the department with one fundamental question: Is it likely to contribute to improved performance for Canadian industry with a high benefit cost yield?
When it comes to specific actions, of course there is no magic formula, no royal road to improved industrial performance. We must work on many fronts-some modest and others rather ambitious. Some will be quick to take effect-others will be much more gradual in their impact. Our work embraces such diverse measures as working with industry in the rationalization and restructuring of an entire industry, the gathering and dissemination of valuable industrial information, the stimulation of research and development, the improvement of industrial design, the fuller utilization of human and natural resources in underemployed regions, the provision of adjustment assistance of both a financial and technical nature, missions abroad to learn from others, the formulation of more and better industrial standards, informed inputs in the formulation of economic policies generally to ensure that the effects on our industrial performance is fully recognized-and in many other areas.
The estimates before you are intended to finance activities in each of these varied fields. These represent only the beginning of the department's work. I intend that each year we will come forward with new programs-some at least of which will be of major significance. The test that I will apply-and I hope that you will accept it as the right test-is the degree to which they contribute to the expansion of efficient production and the improved productivity performance of the Canadian economy.

Mr. Chairman, the minister took some gratification from the success of his department. At the beginning he even said he was gratified, but I should like to take this opportunity to point out that in one area of this responsibility there is nothing he should be happy about. Some encouragement was given in respect of alternative assistance under the Atlantic Development Board, but nothing has been forthcoming except in respect of one or two industrial parks. I hope he will be in a position to answer them because the people in these four cities I have mentioned must have answers very soon.
Will the minister indicate whether federal assistance has been a deciding factor in the location of new industries in the Atlantic provinces, or of assistance in the relocation of industries there? I should like to know whether federal assistance has had any effect in the relocation of an industry in the maritimes. Will the minister also indicate his stand or position in respect of these growth centres? The bill that I put forward this evening is similar in its intent and could be considered auxiliary to the measures I have mentioned. The explanatory notes of the bill say:
The object of this bill is to eliminate the practice whereby insurance companies, commercial corporations and individuals embody in insurance policies, contracts or deeds, fine print clauses excluding their liability under certain circumstances.

(1)	Everyone who, with intent to mislead, prints or causes to print in small typographical character in the body of an insurance policy, contract, deed or other document issued by him or under his authority, clauses concerning payment exclusions or exclusion of responsibility is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars or to a term of imprisonment not exceeding three months or to both fine and imprisonment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on Bill C-ll, an act to amend the Criminal Code (fine print clauses), as proposed and expounded by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather).
I believe at first I should compliment the hon. member on the objectives he proposes to attain in his bill. The purpose of the hon. member in proposing his bill is to eliminate the practice under which insurance companies use fine print clauses to exclude their own liability. I cannot but agree with the explanatory notes, that it is desirable that payment exclusions or exclusion of responsibility be listed plainly and clearly in the body of insurance policies. However, Mr. Speaker, even if I do agree with the object of the bill and the good intentions of the hon. member, I doubt very much whether the results he seeks would be achieved by his bill.
It should be noted that the amendment proposed rests on the intent to mislead. As a matter of fact the first part of the amendment reads as follows: "Everyone who, with intent to mislead, prints...". There are already provisions in the Criminal Code relating to fraud, and these provisions can be used to cover the circumstances contemplated by this amendment, since the intention to
October 27, 1967	COMMONS
mislead is an essential element of both offences.
It should also be pointed out that some of the provincial statutes already cover the area covered by the proposed amendment. For example, section 134, paragraph 2, of the insurance act 1964, revised statutes of Manitoba, chapter 126, provides that when there are exclusion clauses like the one referred to in the proposed amendment, there must be stamped in red ink upon the policy the following words? "This policy contains a limitation of liability clause or clauses".
The second point I wish to raise at this time with regard to the proposed amendment is the reference to printing as being an essential element of the offence. The first portion of the proposed amendment reads as follows: "Everyone who, with intent to mislead, prints or causes to print". In my opinion in order to cover the evil and protect the public it should not be necessary that the offender print or cause to print the document in question; it should be sufficient if he simply issues the document. It would appear to be easier to prove that an insurance company has issued a document than to show that it has printed it.
The third point which would be underlined is that the proposed offence is stated to be an indictable offence. However, the punishment suggested is less than in the case of summary conviction offences as found in section 694 of the Criminal Code of Canada. If it is to fall under the Criminal Code of Canada, I submit it should be a case of summary conviction and not an indictable offence.
However, I personally feel this matter should not be dealt with under the Criminal Code, because there is already a proper and adequate civil remedy. Any person who is misled by fine print in an insurance policy or a contract has a cause for civil action and can receive compensation by way of damages. If a person is not misled by fine print, there would appear to be little point in endeavouring to create a criminal offence.
In any event, it is the provincial legislatures that have jurisdiction over such matters as insurance policies, contracts, deeds, and the like. It is therefore the provincial legislatures that should provide appropriate civil remedies where any person is misled as a result of fine print in a contract. Indeed, it might well be said that legislation of the kind contained in the proposed amendment in Bill Cl-11 will be simply an attempt to control through the Criminal Code a subject which normally falls under provincial jurisdiction.

Perhaps it is not a good policy to attempt to do indirectly what should not be done directly. However, I sympathize with my hon. friend and I agree with him that efforts should be made to curb any attempt to trick the public into buying insurance policies which otherwise they would not buy. The problem was much more acute some 20 years ago. May I refer to an item which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on May 17, 1945, as quoted in a book entitled "Life Insurance Without Exploitation", written by Edwin C. Guillet. I quote from page 69:
"People," says the eminent columnist J. V. McAree, "have to be ordered and frightened at great cost into buying life insurance and saving their money and avoiding body odour and bad breath ... This is something new in history ... an advertising blitz the like of which no other generation has seen:... mass appeals,.. .campaigns and drives and massed propaganda ...
But we think that the total amount of propaganda information tends to debase those who are subjected to this never-ending bombardment... No doubt we shall outlive it and survive, but the process will be painful and perhaps fraught with danger."
We did survive the insurance propaganda bombardment through better information to an enlightened public and also through efforts of the insurance companies to police themselves. For many years now the Canadian Federation of Insurance Agents and Brokers Association has been pressing hard for stricter controls. May I quote a few paragraphs from an article which appeared in the Financial Post on September 17, 1966, carrying the heading "No More Fine Print, Maybe No Policies".
Insurance buyers soon may not have to complain about all that fine print in their car insurance policies. Reason: They may not have policies.

Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to congratulate the member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather) for introducing Bill No. C-ll. He referred, I think, to a point which is most important, in my opinion. More and more, certain companies-I do not want to accuse them of fraud-insert in some contracts clauses written in what is called fine print and which often are important parts of the contracts. I think that the examples given by the member for New Westminster are true and that, in most cases, the contracting parties may not have the legal knowledge necessary to judge the contents of the documents they sign.
I was happy to hear also, and I was not told personally but people in general know, that the department of consumer affairs will look after the protection of the Canadian taxpayer doing business with companies whose amount of business and legal knowledge is much higher than that of the contracting parties.
However, when reading the explanatory notes, one cannot but agree with the hon. member who introduced that bill. In fact, he states that the object of the bill is to eliminate the practice whereby insurance companies, commercial corporations and individuals embody in insurance policies, contracts or deeds, fine print clauses excluding their liability under certain circumstances.
And again in the explanatory notes, our hon. colleague adds that:
It is desirable that payment exclusions or exclusion of responsibility be listed plain and clear in the body of insurance policies, contracts and deeds.
Once again I fully agree with him. Are the amendments proposed by him stringent enough and do they come under the jurisdiction of the federal government?
The bill mentions among others things:
-is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars-
Five hundred dollars-I suppose that amount could be found in the till of a large insurance company...
-or to a term of imprisonment not exceeding three months or to both fine and imprisonment everyone who with intent to mislead-

-and still there must be some evidence. In the case of large insurance company, I wonder who would be imprisoned as I said earlier. And the bill states:
*-prints or causes to print in small typographical character in the body of an insurance policy, contract, deed or other document issued by him or under his authority, clauses concerning payment exclusions or exclusion of responsibility-
I am quite willing to believe that the mover of Bill No. C-ll is sincere. But I wonder how, in its application, we can ever evoke the penalties he himself advocates in the bill.
When we speak of fine print, more than insurance companies are involved. We could go so far as to say that the same problem exists where finance companies are concerned. And the same goes for almost all contracts the consumer must sign, either when he needs protection or when he needs a loan.
Once again, I agree fully with the mover of the bill. I trust the new department established to protect the consumer will pay very special attention to this matter, which is of the greatest importance. Even though this bill is brought in on a Friday night, before the week-end, and most of the members are on their way to their riding, that does not lessen in any way the importance of the matter brought up by the hon. member.
I am sure that not only the members of this house but all the Canadian people agree with him.
Now, does the federal government have jurisdiction in the above matter? My colleague from Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Dube), who is a lawyer-I will not say that I do not have that honour, but rather that I am not in that condition-mentioned that this matter could be within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
For my part, since I come from the province which my hon. colleague from New Westminster knows, I think that if the provinces have jurisdiction over this matter, we would perhaps be wrong in trying to pass legislation before the provinces have had a chance to give their opinion concerning this case.
I think my colleague for Restigouche-Madawaska said that all questions concerning insurance policies, contracts and so on are within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures.
I think that he has also mentioned that the provincial legislatures had the civil power to
October 27, 1967	COMMONS
remedy the problem brought up by the hon. member.
I am not a lawyer, but if this question comes under provincial jurisdiction, the mover of the bill will, at least, have had the merit of having brought up in the federal parliament a most important matter.
And if I say this question is important, it is not simply to flatter the hon. member, it is because I, and probably every member of the house, have had complaints from their electors on this question.
It is true-and I wonder how it happens and it is probably the case of the hon. member-that we are often called upon to sign contracts comprising many pages several of which are illegible, and these pages would be more numerous if the writing was legible and if, let us admit it, the terms were more understandable.
I know, as I said at the start, that the examples given by the hon. members even if they are illustrative may, in certain cases, be real. If a fire starts in a house, for instance, as the hon. member said, the company may disclaim any responsibility if a mouse, unfortunately for the owner, were to chew the electric cable. Or if a condition or a clause of the contract does not provide for the mouse to cut the cable, the owner finds himself simply without a claim with the company even though he has paid his yearly premiums and has complied with the conditions he thought required to have the insurance in force.
I believe that in those cases of insurance, since the bill deals only with insurance, I may be able to give some advice to the hon. member. He could even go further by introducing in other circumstances a similar bill designed to cover finance companies, as I said earlier.
Let us hope, once again, at least I hope so like the hon. member, that the department of consumer affairs will make a point of inquiring carefully in all such situations in order to protect all citizens. It is quite irregular that some companies, more powerful no doubt than the sponsor of the bill and myself, can submit to Canadian taxpayers some contracts that are often misunderstood, but which actually can cause grave prejudice to the contracting party who is acting in good faith.
I should not like what I just said to be construed as an accusation against insurance companies, or against finance companies.

I would not say here that such companies are dishonest, far from it, I just say that the authorities involved, in this case provincial authorities, should see to it that these companies operate in such a way that contracts might be understood by those to whom they sell insurance or finance.
And, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I want to congratulate again the hon. member and I repeat my wish that the new department for consumer protection shall not only be instituted but also become operative as soon as possible.
If I may somewhat digress at this point, though this may not be quite in order, because we are considering a specific bill, I would say that the Canadian people feel, I am sure, that the setting up of such a department is long overdue.
Insurance companies were mentioned this afternoon, and I referred as well to finance companies, but many more areas could be involved. At that time, the head of the department and his senior officials will have the responsibility to protect the people. We are here precisely to protect those who delegated their authority to us, while giving us at the same time the power to amend our laws so that they are better protected.
Again, if we were thereby trespassing on the authority of the provinces and infringing upon their autonomy, as my colleague from Restigouche-Madawaska said, I think it would be not only unfair, but wrong on our part to try to deal with a problem which is not within our jurisdiction.
Therefore, I do not blame the hon. member who introduced the bill, but congratulate him for having drawn the attention of parliament to a case which should interest everyone-for even though the federal parliament is involved here, we are Canadian citizens. The very fact that our attention has been drawn to the problems presented by insurance contracts is already something, and I think it may be a warning of sorts directed to the provincial authorities through their representative in the house.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of the principle enshrined in Bill No. C-ll. I am and always have been a strong believer in insurance. As a matter of fact, in view of conditions today in this modern world and some of the judgments which have been handed down when matters go to

Amendment to Criminal Code court, I believe everybody must have insurance.
I think it is sale to say that the majority of the people who believe in the principle of insurance and who take out insurance policies do so in the belief that they have a certain coverage which is provided by the clauses in large type that are common to all insurance policy forms. But too many people do not read the very fine print. Even if they do, the print is so fine and the wording so complicated that, if they are like me, they do not understand it.
Some 32 years ago I reached the position where I was able to move from a rented home to a home of my own, with a mortgage. I believed in insurance and I got what I thought was complete coverage of my home. However, a few years ago there was a fire at my home, and when it came to settlement I received about one third of what I anticipated receiving, simply because I had not read or had not been able to understand the fine print on my fire insurance policy.
I also have a relative who believes in insurance coverage, and similarly she thought she was completely covered by her insurance. The diamond in one of her rings dropped out and when the claim was considered the fine print revealed that no insurance was payable, and she still has the ring without the diamond.
I give those two personal experiences of people who believe in insurance. In addition, I believe that people should not only know the extend of their coverage but should also know what the insurance company claims are exclusions. It is my belief, Mr. Speaker, that many people would have a greater understanding of their policies or agreements if the exclusion clauses appeared in large type or, as recommended by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford), type of a different colour, so that these clauses would stand out.
I support the principle of the bill now before us and I hope that the recommendation of the hon. member who introduced it will be accepted, namely that instead of the bill being talked out it be referred for study and possible action either to a committee of the house or to the new department.

Mr. Speaker, I think that on the principle of the bill, we are faced to some extent with a sort of painless operation, since all the hon. members who contributed to the debate so far, have indicated that they supported the bill 
and they have showered the sponsor with congratulations while raising some objections.
I too believe that the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather), is looking for perfection and would want, of course, to see it prevail everywhere in the world. Obviously, his intentions are good, but in spite of all the legislation we could pass here, a great many people will still remain extremely gullible.
I should like now to give a few examples just to show the extent of the general public's gullibility with regard to printed matters sent to their homes, whether it be small print or coloured print, or underlined sentences or words in italics and so forth.
It is understandable of course, because everyone is not an intellectual. Those people who have to take insurance policies, for instance, are workers who are not accustomed to reading and most of the time they get confused when they have to follow a text, a little long and a little condensed.
I remember a rather recent case where, for instance, I sent a questionnaire to my constituents. In a rather large committee, we had studied a most simple questionnaire hoping that everyone would understand it quite well. You would be surprised to see how many people-and my electors are not any dumber than those in other ridings in the country-did not understand it. For instance, there were two cards, one had to be detached and the other on which appeared the questions was to be returned to me. There was nothing complicated about it; all they had to do was to detach the card and mail it. However, I would dare say that 40 per cent of those who answered sent both cards back.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
No need for me to labour the point, but it shows that even if we were to pass the bill of the hon. member for New Westminster, requiring that the fine print clauses on insurance policies be printed in larger print, in colour or in italics, some people still would not understand.
You know, it is a law of nature. However hard you try, you will never reach perfection. Somebody, who died a long time ago, used to express this truth in terms that might appear to some as rather crude. He used to say: "There's a sucker born every minute."
Jocular as it may be, it is nevertheless true. There will always be people whose gullibility will get them into trouble. Passing all the laws under heaven will never help in this respect.
