Besides, practically speaking, can you imagine how you would apply this suggestion to the hon. member for New Westminster?
There will always be all sorts of objections and there will always remain people who are clever enough to find means of cheating others. There are experts in that field. However, I do not think that we should carry our legislation too far; we should rather try to make it easier to obtain relief through existing legislation. A moment ago, the member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Dube) said that this is a provincial matter and that people who are wronged should resort to existing legislation.
I would suggest instead that appeal to existing legislation be facilitated to the common people, those I call gullible souls who are liable to be cheated. I speak of gullible souls, but the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who seconded the motion, said himself that he had been cheated, and yet he is one of the most intelligent members of this house. Therefore, imagine what it must be like for those I call gullible souls. It would be advisable to make it easier for them to start court proceedings, to make it so that they will not have to spend too much money in order to retain a lawyer to plead their case; otherwise in most cases they would not see a lawyer and would incur a loss because they failed to read the small print in the insurance policies they signed.
It has been said that this is a provincial matter. It might be. I am not a lawyer. But if there was only that argument to prevent its passing, I would be in favour of the bill which is good in theory, but I just want to say that respect for what is called provincial antonomy must be kept within bounds, although some must be shown. There are some cases where the provinces are unable to exercise their prerogative, then, the federal government would be justified in stepping in, but the people who feel aggrieved may already obtain relief through existing provincial legislation.
Then, I say this, Mr. Chairman, while I associate with the others to congratulate the hon. member for New Westminster for his excellent intentions, we ought to take steps that will make the existing conditions as perfect as possible in order that the ordinary people may not be aggrieved in the process. If we pass this bill, we will have to pass a hundred more to cope with those who specialize in the art of misleading people, and there would never be an end to it all. Therefore, I say, in spite of its fine objective this
Amendment to Criminal Code bill would be extremely difficult to enforce and even if it were possible to enforce it, it would complicate the situation rather than simplify it. As the saying goes, leave well enough alone, which is obvious. I wonder is this is not a case where this really applies.
I noticed that the member said he was only interested in the principle; that if it was passed, we would discuss its application and then endeavour to have it applied in a practical way. Now, I must admit that I would be at a loss to do so; yet, I have a certain experience of those matters, because I have dealt in insurance and even in the printing business for a while. I fail to see how a recommendation like this one could be applied in a practical way, and especially how the companies could be bound by law to comply therewith.
In conclusion, I feel the sponsor of the bill should be commended for having called the attention of the house to a real problem, but which could be solved otherwise, by making it easier to resort to existing statutes, for instance, and, as suggested earlier by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine), by drawing the attention of the new minister of corporations and consumer affairs to any possible abuse. He may succeed, through methods he will have to devise in the coming months, in preventing excessive abuses, even though everything should not be forbidden in the field of publicity which mislead simple people by all kinds of tricks. Even if it were printed in type as large as this, there are still people to write a formula in such a subtle way that most people would not understand it and in this I am supported by the statement of my hon. colleague who, I repeat, is one of the most intelligent members in the house and who admitted that he had himself been misled. Imagine how much influence can be exerted on people with much less experience and education. Even if the type is enlarged they can still mislead them by changing the wording. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I join with the others to congratulate the mover by saying that his intention was excellent and will have a future, because having brought this to our attention, the new minister will surely be able to intervene and possibly the members may bring to the attention of their voters the fact that there is provincial legislation permitting action.

In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is a very good suggestion. But it still does not nullify the other objection I mentioned when I said that there will always be people in this world of ours who specialize in fooling other people. For instance, suppose you print it in red, and suppose I am the president of a big company and I am somewhat of a crook and-I hope this will not be taken for granted-I will hire some learned people who are able to construct a sentence in which the average citizen will see nothing wrong. That is a specialty of people in public relations-and I know something about it, because I am in public relations.
I am trying to do things the right way, the honest way, because I work for small fry, and not for big companies which might believe they could pay me enough to convince me that I should act against my conscience and demonstrate what Barnum once said, that there is a "fish" born every minute. Even if you pass laws to prevent trickery there will always be somebody smart enough to find another trick that will fool the public. I suggest that we should tackle the problem in another way.
We have provincial laws. Let us make it easier for people to have recourse to those laws. Let us advise the minister to devise special measures to educate the public so that they will take advantage of the laws already existing.

I had a card printed, a double card, which I sent to the people in my riding, some 23,000 of them. They were supposed to tear the card in half and send one piece back. We studied the way that the card should be printed and how it should be presented. We studied this with a committee that specializes in such things connected with printing, and the instructions were in big print. Although I was very sure that everybody would understand-and mind you, I do not think my electors are less intelligent than the average electors throughout this country of ours-of those 23,000 cards that I sent, 40 per cent were returned as the double card, unseparated and untorn. This was done, even though the instructions were given in the largest print that we could put on the card.
Therefore I say there is no use passing dozens or hundreds of laws. The more you pass the more you complicate the problem. Try to solve it with the laws you have now, that is my contention.
